title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning, and happy Thanksgiving weekend! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, alternative/integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from PubMed, JAMA/ASCO, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Nature, and clinical-practice guidelines; citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week's theme: the **topical** evidence is sturdier than the **pill** evidence. Prioritize proven skin interventions, and treat oral "longevity" compounds as promising-but-unproven.

- **Topicals that actually have RCTs.** A new meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (1,361 patients) confirms **topical tretinoin** significantly improves both fine and coarse photoaging wrinkles vs. vehicle — still the best-evidenced anti-aging topical. A 2026 split-face RCT (31 adults) found adding a **vitamin C + E + ferulic-acid** serum to **microneedling** roughly tripled improvement in wrinkle scores and elasticity vs. microneedling + placebo.
- **Procedures/devices — manage expectations.** A 2026 split-face study of an integrated **red-light + microneedling** device found *no significant advantage* over either red light or microneedling alone after multiple-testing correction. **Exosome** facials remain early: one small open-label retinal-exosome study showed improvement, but a controlled trial found exosomes merely *non-inferior* to PRP. Bottom line: combination gadgets aren't clearly better than the individual, cheaper modalities yet.
- **Oral compounds — still investigational.** A 2025 *Nature Aging* RCT (50 adults) showed **urolithin A** (1,000 mg/day, 4 weeks) shifted immune-cell profiles toward a younger, less-exhausted phenotype — but a 2026 meta-analysis of 5 muscle trials found effects on strength/endurance **inconclusive** (low GRADE certainty). An **NIH/NIA** urolithin-A glucose-metabolism RCT (NCT06274749) begins recruiting **Nov 30, 2026**. The **PEARL** rapamycin trial showed only *modest, exploratory* benefits (muscle mass, pain in women), not proven geroprotection, and **senolytics** (e.g., dasatinib+quercetin) remain investigational.

Practical framing: a **retinoid + daily sunscreen** regimen is the highest-yield, best-proven anti-aging move. Be skeptical of single-supplement longevity claims and expensive stacked-device facials.

sections.body:
New 2026 trials reinforce HIIT as a **time-efficient** tool for cardio-metabolic health and fat loss in women — with a consistent caveat to **add resistance work** for muscle and strength.

- **Postmenopausal metabolic wins.** A 2026 RCT (45 women, 50–65, overweight/obese; NCT07302191) compared **HIIT**, **concurrent training (CONC = cardio + resistance)**, and control over 12 weeks. Both HIIT and CONC significantly cut body weight, BMI, abdominal fat, triglycerides, LDL, glucose and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) — but **CONC produced greater drops in weight, BMI and body-fat %**, a nudge toward blending intervals with lifting.
- **Intervals beat steady-state for fitness.** A 2026 RCT (32 postmenopausal women with obesity) found **high-intensity interval walking** outperformed moderate-intensity walking for aerobic capacity (6-minute walk), plasma volume and body composition over 10 weeks — intensity matters.
- **But don't drop strength training.** A randomized parallel-arm trial comparing HIIT with **Hatha yoga** in postmenopausal women found **yoga** produced significantly greater gains in **handgrip strength, gait speed and muscle index (ASMI)**, while body-fat changes were similar between groups. HIIT drives cardio and fat loss; it is **not** a reliable standalone builder of muscle/strength.

Bottom line: use HIIT for efficient cardio and metabolic improvement, **pair it with 2+ days/week of resistance training**, progress intensity gradually, and keep recovery adequate — especially around menopause.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Three 2026 trials refine *how* to do it well.

- **Supervision matters.** A 2026 RCT (60 women) found **supervised** PFMT dramatically outperformed **unsupervised/home** PFMT: pad-test leakage fell from 22.9 g to 3.2 g (supervised) vs. only 25.7 g to 17.8 g (home), and 67% vs. 13% reached strong (Oxford grade 4–5) pelvic-floor strength. Home training still helps when supervision isn't available — but confirm technique.
- **PFMT beats Pilates for leakage.** A 3-arm RCT (published Oct 15, 2026; 88 women) compared **PFMT**, **Pilates**, and **Pilates + voluntary pelvic-floor contraction**. PFMT was clearly superior for incontinence impact (ICIQ-SF dropped **−4.4** vs. −0.7 for both Pilates arms) and for squeeze pressure. A separate small postmenopausal trial found PFMT better for *strength* but **not** clearly better for incontinence *severity* vs. cued mat Pilates.
- **Intensity + combined protocols reduce recurrence.** A postpartum SUI trial (99 women) found a **high-intensity combined** PFMT protocol achieved the best strength gains and the **lowest 6-month recurrence** vs. focused (Kegel-only) or generalized training. Adding **progressive muscle relaxation** to PFMT improved comfort in another 2026 four-arm RCT.

Key point: **supervised, correctly-performed, consistent training wins.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; pure reps without technique underperform.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — not a replacement for it. Two themes stand out this week, one targeted and one supportive.

- **A targeted strategy for HER2;TP53 co-mutated tumors.** A new *npj Breast Cancer* study (Oct 15, 2026) explains *why* HER2-mutant cancers that also carry **TP53 (p53) mutations** respond poorly to **neratinib** alone: the p53-mutant tumors ramp up **histone acetylation**, open their chromatin, and hyper-transcribe DNA-repair genes — which makes them **unusually sensitive to the topoisomerase-I payload** in **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)**. In co-mutated mouse/organoid models, **neratinib + T-DXd** was the most effective combination. This combo is in an active **NCI phase-1 trial (NCT05372614)**, now recruiting patients with HER2-altered solid tumors (recommended phase-2 dose established: T-DXd 5.4 mg/kg + neratinib 240 mg/day).
- **Supportive/integrative care with real evidence.** The **SIO–ASCO** guideline recommends **meditation, yoga, music therapy, and relaxation** for anxiety, mood, and quality of life, and **acupressure/acupuncture** for chemo-induced nausea. Crucially, it finds **no strong evidence** that **ingested dietary supplements** improve treatment outcomes — and oral **curcumin did not reduce radiation dermatitis** in a 686-woman RCT; **omega-3s** didn't beat placebo for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain.
- **Lifestyle that moves survival-related outcomes.** A 2026 **ASCO** survivorship review notes the most active survivors had **~28% lower breast-cancer mortality** and **~48% lower all-cause mortality**; guidelines advise **150–300 min/week moderate activity + strength training 2×/week**. Per **WCRF/AICR**, correct **vitamin D** only if deficient — supplements aren't recommended to improve outcomes.

Important framing: targeted combinations like neratinib + T-DXd are **investigational**; integrative therapies are **add-ons** (symptom relief, quality of life, activity) to be coordinated with your oncology team — never substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy. Always screen supplements for **drug interactions**.

sections.body:
For restless, fragmented (sleep-maintenance) insomnia, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I is first-line — sleep hygiene alone is not.** A 2026 *Nature Reviews Disease Primers* overview and a 2026 Australian multi-society position statement both make **CBT-I** the first-line treatment, deliverable in person, by tele-health, or via **self-guided digital** programs. Both stress that general sleep-hygiene tips are **not an adequate stand-alone treatment** for chronic insomnia.
- **For fragmentation specifically, DORAs have the best objective data.** Polysomnography trials of the **dual orexin-receptor antagonist daridorexant** show **dose-dependent reductions in nighttime awakenings (fragmentation)** and more deep (N3) and REM sleep, plus reduced hyperarousal-type EEG features — useful context when the problem is *staying* asleep. Guidelines still reserve **benzodiazepines/Z-drugs for short-term use (≤2–4 weeks)**.
- **Supplements, honestly.** A 2025 RCT of **magnesium bisglycinate** (250 mg elemental, 4 weeks) found only a **small** improvement in insomnia severity (Cohen's d ≈ 0.2) and **no objective** sleep gains; a 2026 systematic review (12 RCTs) rated the evidence **low/very-low certainty** and does **not** support routine magnesium for insomnia. The **VA/DoD 2025** guideline likewise finds **insufficient evidence** for magnesium and recommends **against melatonin** for chronic insomnia (melatonin mainly helps **sleep-onset** and **circadian** problems like jet lag/shift work).

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window; get **morning daylight**.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and start **CBT-I** (in-person or digital) before reaching for medication.
